subject: English
topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative
description: Sentence improvement: identify grammatically or stylistically incorrect underlined phrase, choose the best replacement — subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, idiom, word choice, redundancy.

questions.stem: He is one of those students who (works) hard every day. Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: work — the antecedent of 'who' is 'students' (plural), so plural verb needed
works — treats 'one' as the antecedent, a common but grammatically debated error
has worked — unnecessary shift to present perfect without contextual support
No improvement required — the original 'works' is incorrect here

questions.explanation: RULE: 'one of those + noun + who' — the relative clause 'who' refers to the PLURAL noun ('students'), not 'one'. Therefore the verb after 'who' must be PLURAL: 'work'. CORRECT: 'He is one of those students who WORK hard.' CONTRAST: 'He is the only one of those students who WORKS hard' — here 'the only one' makes the antecedent singular. This is a classic grammar trap in IBPS, SSC, and banking English sections.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: The committee (have decided) to postpone the meeting. Choose the best improvement for the underlined phrase.

options.option_text: has decided — collective nouns acting as a unit take singular verb in formal/Indian English
have decided — this is acceptable in British English but marked wrong in Indian exam context
had been deciding — unnecessary past perfect progressive for a simple decision
No improvement needed — exams expect singular verb for collective noun in Indian English

questions.explanation: RULE (Indian exam standard): collective nouns (committee, jury, team, class, family) acting as a SINGLE UNIT take a SINGULAR verb. 'The committee HAS decided' is the expected answer in IBPS PO, SSC, and state PSC exams. BRITISH ENGLISH NOTE: 'The committee have decided' is acceptable in BrE when members act individually, but Indian competitive exams consistently apply the singular rule. EXAM PATTERN: committee, jury, government, parliament, staff, crew — all singular in Indian English exam answers.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: She told me that she (will finish) the report by Friday. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: would finish — reported speech shifts 'will' to 'would' (sequence of tenses)
will finish — correct in direct speech but wrong after past reporting verb 'told'
had finished — past perfect implies completion before another past event; not appropriate here
should finish — 'should' introduces obligation/recommendation, changing the meaning entirely

questions.explanation: SEQUENCE OF TENSES: when the reporting verb is past ('told'), the reported clause must also shift to a past form. 'will' → 'would'. CORRECT: 'She told me that she WOULD FINISH the report by Friday.' FULL SHIFT TABLE: am/is→was; are→were; has/have→had; will→would; can→could; may→might; shall→should. EXCEPTION: universal truths and reported questions keep present tense ('He said that the Earth is round'). PYQ: sequence-of-tenses in indirect speech is heavily tested in IBPS PO/Clerk English.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: Neither the manager nor the employees (was) aware of the new policy. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: were — with neither…nor, verb agrees with the nearer subject ('employees', plural)
was — applies singular agreement to 'manager' (the farther subject) by mistake
are — wrong tense; past context requires past verb form here (not this)
have been — present perfect is incompatible with the past-tense context of the sentence

questions.explanation: NEITHER…NOR RULE: verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST (nearer) to the verb. Here: 'the manager' (singular) OR 'the employees' (plural) — 'employees' is nearer → WERE. CORRECT: 'Neither the manager nor the employees WERE aware.' EITHER…OR works the same way. MEMORY TRICK: 'ProxiMate rule' — agree with the proximate (nearest) subject. IBPS/SSC PATTERN: this is one of the top-tested neither/nor/either/or agreement rules.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: The news (are) shocking to all of us. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: is — 'news' is a singular uncountable noun in English despite ending in -s
are — treats 'news' as plural due to the -s ending, which is incorrect
were — past tense inappropriate when no past context is established in the sentence
have been — present perfect progressive does not fit a state expressed by an adjective

questions.explanation: SINGULAR UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS ENDING IN -S: news, mathematics, physics, economics, athletics, billiards, measles, mumps — all take SINGULAR verbs. 'The news IS shocking.' Other examples: 'Mathematics IS difficult.' 'Physics IS my favourite subject.' PLURAL EXCEPTION: 'The goods ARE ready' (goods = countable plural). EXAM SHORTCUT: if the -s noun refers to a subject of study or a concept treated as a single entity, it's singular.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: He is used to (work) late in the office. Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: working — 'used to + VERB-ing' means accustomed to; -ing form required after preposition 'to'
work — confuses 'used to work' (past habit) with 'be used to working' (accustomed to)
have worked — present perfect after 'to' is ungrammatical in this structure
No improvement needed — 'work' after 'used to' is the past-habit form, not this structure

questions.explanation: TWO DIFFERENT STRUCTURES: (1) USED TO + bare infinitive = past habit that no longer happens. 'He used to WORK late' (he no longer does). (2) BE/GET USED TO + V-ing = accustomed to (can be present or past). 'He IS USED TO WORKING late' (he is accustomed to it now). The sentence says 'He is used to...' so structure (2) applies → gerund 'working'. EXAM TRAP: this distinction between the two 'used to' structures is tested in nearly every IBPS PO/Clerk English paper.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: The teacher, as well as her students, (are) attending the seminar. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: is — 'as well as' is a parenthetical addition; the main subject 'the teacher' (singular) governs the verb
are — treats 'the teacher + students' as a compound subject joined by 'and', which is incorrect
were — tense change unjustified without past-time context in the sentence (not this)
have been — aspect change inappropriate for a simple ongoing state or action (not this)

questions.explanation: PARENTHETICAL ADDITION RULE: phrases like 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with', 'in addition to', 'besides', 'accompanied by' — when inserted between subject and verb — do NOT change the number of the verb. VERB AGREES with the MAIN (grammatical) subject alone. 'The teacher' = singular → IS. CONTRAST: 'The teacher AND her students are attending' — here 'and' creates a compound subject → plural verb. PYQ: 'as well as' agreement appears in virtually every IBPS PO/Clerk session-1 or session-2 English paper.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative

questions.stem: The bread, along with the butter, (were) left on the table. Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: are, showing a present-tense plural verb form
was, since the true subject 'bread' is singular
have been, for a present perfect plural usage
had been, using a past perfect tense here

questions.explanation: 'Along with' is a parenthetical phrase, not a conjunction like 'and', so the verb agrees with the actual subject 'bread' (singular) — 'was' is correct. 'Were' and 'have been' wrongly treat 'butter' as a co-subject. This is a classic SSC trap: only 'and' creates a compound plural subject.

questions.stem: Of the two candidates, she is (the most suitable) for the senior position. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: the most suitable, as she surpasses all other candidates
more suitable, since only two people are being compared
much suitable, adding an intensifier to the adjective
the better suited, mixing superlative with comparative form

questions.explanation: When comparing exactly two items, the comparative degree ('more suitable') is used, not the superlative ('most suitable'). Superlative applies only when three or more are compared. 'Much suitable' is non-standard, and 'the better suited' is awkward phrasing.

questions.stem: If I (would have known) about the seminar, I would have registered on time. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: would have known, expressing a past unfulfilled possibility
had known, for a correct third conditional if-clause
would know, using the simple present conditional form
have known, using the present perfect in the if-clause

questions.explanation: In a Type-3 (third) conditional, the if-clause requires the past perfect ('had known'), not 'would have known'. The 'would have' form belongs only in the result clause. Using 'would have' in the if-clause is the single most common conditional error in SSC/IBPS papers.

questions.stem: The two business partners decided to divide all responsibilities between (one another). Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: one another, for mutual action among a group of two
each other, as the reference is to exactly two people
themselves, as a reflexive pronoun for both subjects
the other person, referring to the second individual only

questions.explanation: 'Each other' is the standard choice when exactly two persons are involved; 'one another' is used for three or more. Since only two partners are mentioned, 'each other' is correct. The reflexive 'themselves' changes the meaning (individual action, not mutual exchange).

questions.stem: She left for her hometown three years (before). Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: ago, counting time backward from the present moment
before, indicating time prior to a specific past event
back, used informally as a substitute for past duration
earlier, to specify a preceding but indefinite time point

questions.explanation: 'Ago' measures time backward from the present and pairs with the simple past tense — 'left three years ago' is correct. 'Before' is used when measuring back from a specific past event, not the present. 'Back' is informal and non-standard in formal writing; 'earlier' requires a reference point to be meaningful.

questions.stem: Hardly (he had) stepped onto the stage when the crowd began cheering loudly. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: he had, keeping the standard subject-before-auxiliary order
had he, as inversion is mandatory after 'Hardly' at the start
had he been, adding a progressive aspect after the inversion
he was, replacing with simple past and no inversion used

questions.explanation: When 'Hardly', 'Scarcely', or 'No sooner' opens a sentence, subject-auxiliary inversion is obligatory: 'Hardly had he stepped…'. This mirrors negative inversion rules. 'Had he been' incorrectly introduces progressive aspect; 'he was' destroys both the inversion rule and the tense ('Hardly…when' requires past perfect in the first clause).

questions.stem: The principal insisted that every student (submits) the project before the deadline. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: submits, applying third-person singular present agreement
submit, using the mandative subjunctive base form required
should submits, pairing a modal with an inflected verb form
must be submitting, using modal progressive for added urgency

questions.explanation: After verbs of insistence, demand, or recommendation (insist, suggest, demand, recommend), the mandative subjunctive requires the bare infinitive regardless of subject — 'submit', not 'submits'. 'Submits' is the tempting trap because 'every student' is third-person singular, but subjunctive mood overrides standard agreement. 'Should submits' is doubly wrong: a modal must be followed by a base verb, never an inflected one.

questions.stem: She (has completed) the assignment before the teacher collected it. Choose the best improvement for the underlined part.

options.option_text: She has completed the assignment before the teacher collected it.
She completed the assignment before the teacher collected it.
She had completed the assignment before the teacher collected it.
She was completing the assignment before the teacher collected it.

questions.explanation: C is correct because when two actions both occurred in the past and one happened before the other, the earlier action takes the past perfect tense ('had completed'). 'Has completed' (present perfect) is wrong when a specific past time reference is implied by the narrative context. Option B (simple past 'completed') is tempting but less precise — formal English prefers past perfect to signal the sequence of two distinct past events.

questions.stem: Mount Everest is (more higher) than any other peak in the world. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: Mount Everest is most higher than any other peak in the world.
Mount Everest is the most highest peak than others in the world.
Mount Everest is higher than any other peak in the world.
Mount Everest is more high than any other peak in the world.

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'more higher' is a double comparative — using both the adverb 'more' and the comparative suffix '-er' simultaneously is a grammatical error. The simple comparative 'higher' alone is sufficient. Option A ('most higher') commits the same category of error. Option D ('more high') is also wrong: 'high' forms its comparative as 'higher', never 'more high'.

questions.stem: If it (will rain) tomorrow, we will postpone the outdoor ceremony. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: If it will rain tomorrow, we will postpone the outdoor ceremony.
If it rains tomorrow, we will postpone the outdoor ceremony.
If it rained tomorrow, we will postpone the outdoor ceremony.
If it would rain tomorrow, we will postpone the outdoor ceremony.

questions.explanation: B is correct because in a Type 1 (real/open) conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple tense ('rains'), not the future tense ('will rain'). The main clause correctly retains 'will postpone'. Option C ('rained') belongs to Type 2 hypothetical conditionals, which would then require 'would postpone' in the main clause — mixing a Type 2 if-clause with a Type 1 main clause creates a tense inconsistency that examiners specifically target.

questions.stem: The responsibility of completing the project on time lies on you and (I). Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: The responsibility of completing the project on time lies on you and I.
The responsibility of completing the project on time lies on you and me.
The responsibility of completing the project on time lies on you and myself.
The responsibility of completing the project on time lies on you and mine.

questions.explanation: B is correct because after a preposition ('on'), the objective case pronoun 'me' is required, not the nominative 'I'. A useful test: remove 'you and' — 'lies on I' is obviously ungrammatical, confirming 'me'. Option C ('myself') is a reflexive/emphatic pronoun, valid only when the subject of the clause is also the speaker ('I did it myself'), which is not the case here. Option A is the most common spoken-English error and the primary distractor.

questions.stem: No sooner did the curtain rise (when) the audience burst into applause. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: No sooner did the curtain rise when the audience burst into applause.
No sooner did the curtain rise than the audience burst into applause.
No sooner did the curtain rise before the audience burst into applause.
No sooner did the curtain rise until the audience burst into applause.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'No sooner' is always paired with 'than' as a fixed correlative conjunction: 'No sooner...than'. The confusion arises because the parallel structure 'Hardly/Scarcely...when/before' uses 'when' — candidates incorrectly apply 'when' to 'No sooner' by analogy. Options C and D ('before', 'until') are never paired with 'No sooner' in standard English grammar.

questions.stem: I wish I (was) invited to the felicitation ceremony held last month. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: I wish I was invited to the felicitation ceremony held last month.
I wish I were invited to the felicitation ceremony held last month.
I wish I had been invited to the felicitation ceremony held last month.
I wish I would be invited to the felicitation ceremony held last month.

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'I wish' referring to a past event ('held last month') requires the past perfect tense ('had been invited') to express an unfulfilled wish about the past. Option B ('were') is the present subjunctive used for present/hypothetical wishes only ('I wish I were taller') — it cannot refer to a completed past event. Option A ('was') is doubly wrong: it uses indicative mood and the wrong tense for any wish construction.

questions.stem: Had he studied regularly, he (will pass) the examination with distinction. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: Had he studied regularly, he will pass the examination with distinction.
Had he studied regularly, he would pass the examination with distinction.
Had he studied regularly, he would have passed the examination with distinction.
Had he studied regularly, he could pass the examination with distinction.

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'Had he studied' is an inverted Type 3 conditional — equivalent to 'If he had studied' (past unreal). In Type 3 conditionals, the result clause requires 'would have + past participle' ('would have passed'). Option B ('would pass') is the result clause for Type 2 conditionals (present hypothetical) and is incompatible with the inverted past-perfect if-clause. Option A ('will pass') is a Type 1 result clause — an impossible mismatch with a past unreal condition.
